extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, researchers, and practitioners interested in administrative law and judicial review
extracted.subtask_description: A Ballotpedia encyclopedia-style summary of the Supreme Court decision in Vermont Yankee v. NRDC, explaining the Court's limits on judicial intervention in agency procedures and the decision's implications for administrative law. The page provides background, quotes from the opinion, and commentary on the ruling's impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts may not impose additional procedural requirements on agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court set a clear and definitive precedent that courts could not impose additional procedural requirements on agencies, they could only evaluate existing procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Rehnquist characterized the D.C. Appeals Court's actions as "an unjustifiable intrusion into the administrative process," cautioning against reviewing courts "engrafting their own notions of proper procedures upon agencies entrusted with substantive functions by Congress." The Supreme Court reversed the D.C. Circuit for exceeding its authority and remanded for review within the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review limited to conformity with established procedures, not outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review could only concern itself with the agency's success or failure to conform to the established procedures; it could not invalidate an action simply because the court was "unhappy with the result reached."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court guidance emphasizes that review focuses on whether statutory procedural requirements were met, not whether judges prefer a different substantive outcome. Administrative decisions should be set aside only for substantial procedural or substantive reasons mandated by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA's mandate is essentially procedural — ensure a fully informed decision
rubrics_metrics.description: NEPA does set forth significant substantive goals for the Nation, but its mandate to the agencies is essentially procedural... It is to insure a fully informed and well-considered decision, not necessarily a decision the judges ... would have reached had they been members of the decisionmaking unit of the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page quotes the opinion to show NEPA requires process (adequate environmental impact consideration) rather than guaranteeing a particular substantive result; courts should review whether the process was adequate under NEPA, not substitute their own substantive judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative decisions may be set aside only for substantial statutory reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative decisions should be set aside ... only for substantial procedural or substantive reasons as mandated by statute (citing Consolo v. FMC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard limits judicial intervention to cases where statutory requirements were not met or where substantive statutory grounds exist; mere dissatisfaction with results or peripheral issues is not enough to overturn agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor or peripheral oversights do not justify overturning exhaustive agency proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A single alleged oversight on a peripheral issue, urged by parties who never fully cooperated or indeed raised the issue below, must not be made the basis for overturning a decision properly made after an otherwise exhaustive proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion warns against nullifying long, thorough agency proceedings for isolated or peripheral mistakes; the Consumers Power example is used to illustrate how later invalidation based on minor references can be inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for constitutional constraints or extremely compelling circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court explicitly created a "constitutional constraints or extremely compelling circumstances" exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly commentary (Professor Neely) notes lower courts might develop this exception or otherwise sidestep Vermont Yankee in rare cases that implicate constitutional issues or very compelling circumstances; the exception indicates the rule against imposing procedures is not absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing courts may challenge agency characterizations of exemptions from notice-and-comment (section 553)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower courts can sidestep Vermont Yankee by ... refusing to accept agencies' characterization of some rules as exempt from the notice and comment requirements of section 553 of the Administrative Procedure Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies an area of tension: courts may scrutinize agency claims that certain actions are exempt from APA notice-and-comment obligations, potentially requiring procedural safeguards despite Vermont Yankee's general rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand must direct review within the bounds of the Administrative Procedure Act
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court remanded the decision regarding Vermont Yankee's license to the Appeals Court to review again, within the bounds of the Administrative Procedure Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a higher court finds prior review improper, any remand should instruct the lower court to reassess agency action consistent with the APA's procedural and substantive limits rather than imposing extra-procedural requirements.
